draft.title: Hindu bioethics
card: Bioethics asks what is right in medicine and the care of life. Hindu views on issues such as euthanasia (ending a life to relieve suffering) draw on several teachings.
Ahimsa
the principle of non-harm. Many Hindus hold that deliberately ending a life, even a suffering one, causes harm and so goes against ahimsa.
Karma
actions have consequences, and suffering may be linked to past actions. Many Hindus believe that cutting life short does not remove karma, which may carry into a future life.
Duty to preserve life
life is seen as sacred, and caring for the sick and dying is a duty. For this reason, many Hindus oppose euthanasia, though views can vary between communities.
draft.remember: Ahimsa, karma and the duty to preserve life lead many Hindus to oppose euthanasia.

a.q: Which teaching leads many Hindus to oppose euthanasia because it is seen as an act of harm?
opts: Ahimsa, the principle of non-harm
Karma, the idea that actions are always rewarded
Samsara, the idea that life is an illusion
Dharma, the rule that illness must be endured
a.why: Ahimsa means non-harm, and many Hindus see deliberately ending a life as harm. Karma is about the consequences of actions, not a rule that actions are rewarded, so it is a less direct match for this reason.
a.clue: Think of the teaching that means non-harm.

b.q: Dev's grandmother is dying in pain. Dev says that ending her life early would not free her from her karma. Which Hindu belief is he drawing on?
opts: Karma may carry into a future life, so it is not escaped
Ahimsa allows harm if it ends suffering sooner
Life has no worth once a person is in great pain
Caring for the sick is a duty only for doctors
b.why: Dev is applying karma: consequences of actions may continue into a future life, so cutting life short does not remove them. The ahimsa option is wrong because ahimsa is the principle of non-harm and does not permit harm to end suffering.
b.clue: Dev talks about consequences that may not end with death.

b.best: Karma may carry into a future life, so it is not escaped

problems.detail: The stem says 'an act of harm', which matches 'non-harm' in the right option, and the clue ('the teaching that means non-harm') gives the answer away outright.
The distractors use 'always' (karma) and 'must' (dharma), absolutes the card does not use. They make the unqualified right option stand out as the only accurate-sounding one.

The distractor 'Samsara, the idea that life is an illusion' misdefines samsara, which is the cycle of birth, death and rebirth; illusion is closer to maya. A Year 12 student could take away a false definition.
Why (a) calls karma 'a less direct match', which suggests the karma option is partly right. That option is simply wrong: it misdefines karma as 'actions are always rewarded'.
The stem names karma, and the right option is the only one that mentions karma. It is also the only one with the hedge 'may', so a student can pick it without knowing the idea.
The distractor 'a duty only for doctors' uses 'only', an absolute that marks it as wrong.

proposal.title: Hindu bioethics
card: Bioethics asks what is right in medicine and the care of life. Hindu views on issues such as euthanasia (ending a life to relieve suffering) draw on several teachings.
Ahimsa
the principle of non-harm. Many Hindus hold that deliberately ending a life, even a suffering one, causes harm and so goes against ahimsa.
Karma
actions have consequences, and suffering may be linked to past actions. Many Hindus believe that cutting life short does not remove karma, which may carry into a future life.
Duty to preserve life
life is seen as sacred, and caring for the sick and dying is a duty. For this reason, many Hindus oppose euthanasia, though views can vary between communities.
proposal.remember: Ahimsa, karma and the duty to preserve life lead many Hindus to oppose euthanasia.

a.q: In the view many Hindus hold, how does ahimsa apply to euthanasia?
opts: Deliberately ending a life causes harm, so it breaks ahimsa
Ending a life relieves suffering, so it fulfils ahimsa
Ahimsa applies to animals, so it does not cover euthanasia
Ahimsa means past actions bring results, so pain is earned
a.why: Ahimsa is the principle of non-harm, and many Hindus see deliberately ending a life as a harm, even when the person is suffering. The idea that relieving suffering fulfils ahimsa reverses this view, and the idea that past actions bring results describes karma, not ahimsa.
a.clue: Recall what the word ahimsa means.

b.q: Dev's grandmother is dying in pain. Dev says that ending her life early would not free her from the results of her past actions. Which teaching is he drawing on?
opts: Karma, since its effects may carry into a future life
Karma, since its effects may end when the body dies
Ahimsa, since ending a life may count as harm
Duty to preserve life, since life may be seen as sacred
b.why: Dev's reason is about the results of past actions continuing after death, which is how many Hindus understand karma. The option saying karma ends when the body dies is tempting because it names karma, but it is the opposite of Dev's point. Ahimsa and the duty to preserve life can also lead to opposing euthanasia, but neither is the reason Dev gives.
b.clue: Focus on the reason Dev gives, not just his conclusion.
